- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

mode.description: 'check' (default): if ONBOARDING.md is present locally, uploads it to the most-recent guide (creates one if none exist); otherwise reports the existing link without uploading. 'update': upload to a specific guide by short_code. 'create': always make a new link. 'delete': remove a guide.

short_code.description: Short code of a specific guide to target (returned by a previous call). Honored by check, update, and delete — skips the org-wide lookup and targets this guide directly.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

# Static Analysis Report — AA91901CCE91F160E64B6187EF96EBE5

**Verdict:** MALWARE — trojanized, Intel-signed DLL (`ForOps.dll`) acting as a **DLL-sideloading shellcode loader** (encrypted payload file + module stomping)
**Confidence:** High
**Analysis type:** Static only (Ghidra headless MCP, DIE, FLOSS, custom Python parsers). Nothing was executed or loaded.

---

## 1. Metadata

| Field | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| MD5 | AA91901CCE91F160E64B6187EF96EBE5 | [CONFIRMED] |
| SHA256 | 8E8F0DA12204B277539590DDD30A78CE3943355FD1F8BD9DB71E4272BE71C4BC | [CONFIRMED] |
| Size | 1,174,624 bytes | [CONFIRMED] |
| Type | PE32+ x64 DLL, image base 0x180000000, 9 sections (.text .rdata .data .pdata .00cfg .trace _RDATA .rsrc .reloc), clang/LLVM (Intel oneAPI toolchain) | Ghidra / header parse |
| Version info | Intel Corporation, "Intel(R) Fortran Utility Package", Product "Intel(R) Fortran Compiler Integration", OriginalFilename `ForOps.dll`, 2025.1.1.0; internal export name `ForOps_v17.dll` | VersionInfo, export dir |
| PE timestamp | 2025-03-28 13:59:29 UTC | header |
| Authenticode | **HashMismatch.** Signer `CN=Intel Corporation`, serial 2CC006D7585062D46960F2EB4472150F, thumbprint 5E4AE5E468F6D28D90C48DB09DCB672C2AD5EE4D, issuer Sectigo Public Code Signing CA R36, validity 2025-01-08 → 2026-01-09; timestamp 2025-03-28 14:03:16 UTC (Sectigo TSA R35) | Get-AuthenticodeSignature, PKCS#7 decode |
| Signed digest vs actual | Signed SpcIndirectData SHA256 `9FED12F966464A7D60BDB4EB04F319EB1F5DAA18D0A6E201D793AF54A986EE75` ≠ computed Authenticode SHA256 `10F063745CAFD4A54A9FADEB3C038F9310999AAB95AC145587A800029ED8FC48` | authhash.py [CONFIRMED] |
| PE checksum | stored 0x126A03 ≠ computed 0x128FD2 | [CONFIRMED] |
| Overlay | none (cert table ends at EOF) | [CONFIRMED] |

**Interpretation:** A genuine Intel build, signed 4 minutes after linking, whose signed sections were later edited. The original signature was left in place so the file still looks "Intel-signed" in casual checks. [CONFIRMED tamper; INFERRED intent]

## 2. Ranked findings

1. **[CONFIRMED] Code stomping over exported Fortran-operator functions (`.text` RVA 0x55F0–0x5D6F, ~1.9 KB).**
   - `.pdata` still describes 20 tiny original functions (64–69 bytes each) at 0x5790, 0x57E0, …, 0x5D50: `and_*`, `or_*`, `xor_*`, `eqv_*` × int/log1/log2/log4/log8. Every one of those starts now falls **mid-instruction** in a new, contiguous function.
   - The export `uminus_cplx32` (0x1800055F0) was also replaced.
   - Normal code resumes at 0x5DA0.
   - Evidence: `pdata_gaps.py`/`export_prologues.py` output, Ghidra disassembly.
2. **[CONFIRMED] Anti-sandbox CPU-burn at 0x1800055F0** (export `uminus_cplx32`). It builds a 256-dword table (XOR/`pmulld`, constants 0xF0FA2D3D, 0xA93EA2BD), then runs an RC4-like mixing loop 0x509 × 0x155698 ≈ **1.8 × 10⁹ iterations** and discards the result. It's the first thing the loader calls.
3. **[CONFIRMED] Shellcode loader at 0x180005760** (unexported, unreferenced inside the DLL), reconstructed by disassembly in a writable Ghidra copy:
   1. `call 0x1800055F0` (delay)
   2. `GetModuleHandleW(L"kernel32")` (IAT 0x180108668)
   3. Walks the kernel32 export table and resolves APIs by **custom hash `h = h*2 + c`, seed 0x0761F9B7** (hash loop at 0x180005800)
   4. `LocalAlloc(0, 0x05C157E5)` (~96 MB buffer)
   5. `GetModuleFileNameW(NULL, buf, 0x5CA)` (IAT 0x180108648), cut at the last `\` → **host EXE folder**
   6. `SetCurrentDirectoryW(folder)`
   7. `CreateFileA("compiler128.sys", GENERIC_READ, FILE_SHARE_READ, NULL, 4, 3, NULL)`
   8. `GetFileSize`; if 0 → **`TerminateProcess(-1, 1)`**
   9. `ReadFile` the whole file
   10. Blob at file offset **0x4D42**: dword count + dword key; **additive dword decode** (`add [rcx], r8d` loop at 0x180005B40)
   11. `LoadLibraryA(<module name from decoded blob>)`, a **sacrificial DLL**
   12. `VirtualProtect(module.BaseOfCode, len, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE)` → copy decoded shellcode over the module's code → `VirtualProtect` restore → **`call module.BaseOfCode + entry_offset`**, passing a struct {ptr, L"console-io.yaml", 1}
   - This is **module stomping** (T1055 variant): the payload runs from the image-backed memory of a legitimate DLL.
4. **[CONFIRMED] Injected config in `.data`.** A packed, unaligned structure at 0x18010D2CF–0x18010D347 (seed, hashes, sizes, offsets, pointers). The string `console-io.yaml` is written **over entries of the `MY_FOPS` function-pointer table** (0x18010C521) and `compiler128.sys` is at 0x18010D72E. The DLL can no longer work as genuine Intel ForOps, which supports a single-purpose sideload vehicle. [INFERRED]
5. **[CONFIRMED] Everything else matches the genuine Intel runtime.** `DllMain` (0x18009B5C8) is `mov eax,1; ret`; the CRT/`_initterm` initializers (0x18004B8F0, 0x180059960, 0x18009C3D0, 0x1800AA8B0, 0x1800B54E0, 0x1800B9110) are Intel Fortran RTL code (`for_rtl_ICAF_INIT`, `PIN_*`/`FOR_*` env vars, libirc CPU feature init). The `.trace` section is Intel traceback data. Imports (KERNEL32 + IMAGEHLP) are unchanged.
6. **[HYPOTHESIS] Trigger.** Nothing in the DLL references 0x180005760: no rel32, no RIP-relative, no absolute pointer, no RVA, not in an export, `MY_FOPS`, CFG or TLS. It's probably reached by a host application that loads this DLL from its own folder (sideloading) and calls a stomped export. The loader's anchoring to the host EXE's directory supports this. The exact host and export need dynamic confirmation.
7. capa: **UNAVAILABLE** (`memory allocation of 4025952 bytes failed`, low disk/memory at run time). PEstats: **UNAVAILABLE** (`pefile` missing). FLOSS ran: 12,730 static strings, 2 decoded, 16 tight, nothing beyond the items above.
8. No text addressed to an AI was found.

| 0x18009B5C8 | DllMain | Genuine: returns 1 |

| **0x1800055F0** | `uminus_cplx32` → **anti_sandbox_delay** | Injected: ~1.8 B-iteration mixing loop |
| **0x180005760** | **injected_loader_main** | Injected: API hashing, payload file read/decode, module stomping, execute |
| 0x180005800 (loop) | api_hash | `h = h*2 + c`, seed 0x0761F9B7 |
| 0x180005B40 (loop) | blob_decode | dword += key |
| 0x18010D2CF–0x18010D347 | loader_config | Packed config (in .data) |

|---|---|
| 0xFA15E7B5 | TerminateProcess |
| 0x87E844A1 | LocalAlloc |
| 0xA1392D69 | SetCurrentDirectoryW |
| 0x0FD07183 | CreateFileA |
| 0x0FD068A5 | GetFileSize |
| 0x61FA10B1 | ReadFile |
| 0x1FA10BA3 | LoadLibraryA |
| 0x7E86209E | VirtualProtect |

## 4. IOCs

| Type | Value | Source offset |
|---|---|---|
| SHA256 (this DLL) | 8E8F0DA12204B277539590DDD30A78CE3943355FD1F8BD9DB71E4272BE71C4BC | — |
| MD5 | AA91901CCE91F160E64B6187EF96EBE5 | — |
| Filename on disk (likely) | `ForOps.dll` (internal `ForOps_v17.dll`) | VersionInfo / export dir |
| **Payload file (same dir as host EXE)** | `compiler128.sys` | VA 0x18010D72E (file 0x10BB2E) |
| Payload argument string | `console-io.yaml` | VA 0x18010C521 (file 0x10A921) |
| Payload blob offset / decode | offset 0x4D42 in `compiler128.sys`; dword count + additive key | config 0x18010D32F |
| API hash seed / algorithm | 0x0761F9B7; `h = h*2 + c` | 0x18010D2F3 / 0x180005800 |
| Loader allocation size | 0x05C157E5 | 0x18010D337 |
| Forged-signature cert (genuine Intel, abused) | thumbprint 5E4AE5E468F6D28D90C48DB09DCB672C2AD5EE4D; signed digest 9FED12F9…EE75 | cert table 0x11BE00 |

## 5. MITRE ATT&CK

- T1574.002 Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading [INFERRED from design]
- T1036.001 Masquerading: Invalid Code Signature (tampered Intel-signed DLL) [CONFIRMED]
- T1027 / T1140 Obfuscated Files / Deobfuscate: encrypted payload file, additive decode [CONFIRMED]
- T1106 Native API + API hashing (T1027.007 Dynamic API Resolution) [CONFIRMED]
- T1055 Process Injection (module stomping into a sacrificial DLL in-process) [CONFIRMED]
- T1497.003 Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: Time-Based Evasion (CPU-burn delay) [CONFIRMED]

## 6. Alternative hypotheses

| Hypothesis | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Benign corruption / repackaging | **Rejected**: the change is a coherent, compiled loader with API hashing and module stomping, not random damage |
| Legitimate Intel patch / instrumentation | **Rejected**: Intel would re-sign; the code reads an external `.sys`-named blob and executes it RWX |
| Red-team / pentest tooling | Possible origin, but functionally it is a malicious loader. The verdict stays MALWARE |
| Side-load proxy | Fits: it keeps the genuine export surface so a host can still bind to it |

## 7. Limitations

- No clean `ForOps.dll` 2025.1.1.0 was available offline for a byte-diff. The tampered region was found structurally (`.pdata` vs instruction-boundary mismatch, export prologues, config cross-references). Other small edits elsewhere can't be fully ruled out.
- The payload (`compiler128.sys`) and the sacrificial DLL name (stored inside the encrypted blob) were not available.
- The trigger/host application is not identified statically (finding 6).
- capa and PEstats were unavailable (see 2.7).

## 8. Next steps

1. Hunt for **`compiler128.sys`** and `console-io.yaml` next to any EXE that loads `ForOps.dll` / `ForOps_v17.dll`. Use the decode routine above (offset 0x4D42, count + additive key) to extract the shellcode statically.
2. Get the genuine Intel oneAPI 2025.1.1 `ForOps.dll` and diff it to confirm the exact modified range (expected: .text 0x55F0–0x5D6F, .data around 0x10C521 and 0x10D2CF–0x10D347, 0x10D72E).
3. Identify the host EXE (parent folder of the DLL on the endpoint) and which export it calls.
4. Recommended dynamic analysis (not performed): run the host + DLL + payload in an isolated VM; break on `VirtualProtect` / `LoadLibraryA`; dump the stomped module's `.text` after the copy.

## 9. Detection guidance

- File: Intel-signed `ForOps*.dll` with **Authenticode HashMismatch** (high-fidelity for this pattern).
- Byte pattern (hash loop): `0F B6 C0 48 8D 49 01 8D 14 50 0F B6 01 84 C0 75 EF` plus seed dword `B7 F9 61 07`.
- Behaviour: a process loads `ForOps.dll` from a non-Intel path, reads `compiler128.sys` from its own directory, then makes `VirtualProtect` RWX calls on another module's code section.

| Type | Value | Offset |
|---|---|---|
| SHA256 | 8E8F0DA12204B277539590DDD30A78CE3943355FD1F8BD9DB71E4272BE71C4BC | — |

| Abused Intel cert | 5E4AE5E468F6D28D90C48DB09DCB672C2AD5EE4D | cert table 0x11BE00 |

T1574.002 DLL Side-Loading [INFERRED] · T1036.001 Invalid Code Signature [CONFIRMED] · T1027/T1140 encrypted payload + decode [CONFIRMED] · T1027.007 Dynamic API Resolution [CONFIRMED] · T1055 module stomping [CONFIRMED] · T1497.003 time-based evasion [CONFIRMED]

- Benign corruption: rejected (coherent compiled loader).
- Intel patch: rejected (no re-sign; executes external blob RWX).
- Red-team tooling: possible origin, but it is still malicious in function.
- Side-load proxy: fits.

No clean Intel ForOps.dll 2025.1.1.0 for a byte-diff, so the region was found structurally and other small edits can't be ruled out. The payload `compiler128.sys` and the sacrificial DLL name are unavailable. The host/trigger is not identified. capa/PEstats unavailable.

2. Diff against the genuine oneAPI 2025.1.1 DLL.
3. Identify the host EXE.
4. Dynamic analysis (not performed): isolated VM, break on VirtualProtect/LoadLibraryA, dump the stomped module.

## 9. Detection

- Intel-signed ForOps*.dll with Authenticode HashMismatch.

# Skill: Detecting code-stomped (trojanized) signed DLLs statically

Generic and reusable. No sample-specific IOCs.

## 1. Signature integrity first
- `Get-AuthenticodeSignature` → **HashMismatch** on a vendor-signed binary means the signed bytes were edited after signing. Confirm by recomputing:
  - the Authenticode hash (skip CheckSum, the Security dir entry and the cert table; hash header + sections in raw order) and compare it with the SpcIndirectData digest decoded from the PKCS#7;
  - the PE checksum (a mismatch corroborates post-link edits).
- Check the overlay. If there is none, the change is *inside* sections.
- Expired-cert "NotTimeValid" is irrelevant when a valid timestamp exists. Read dates in the right locale (MM/dd vs dd/MM).

## 2. Find the edited region without a clean copy
- **.pdata vs code mismatch (x64):** RUNTIME_FUNCTION begin addresses that now land mid-instruction (bytes before them are live code, not CC/NOP padding), or a run of tiny original entries covered by one big function, is a strong stomping signal.
- **Export prologue histogram:** classify the first 4 bytes of every export. Compiler-consistent prologues cluster; stomped exports show random mid-instruction bytes. Also flag `E9`, `FF 25`, `mov reg,imm64; jmp reg`, `push; ret`.
- **.pdata-uncovered gaps:** list .text gaps without unwind entries. Leaf CRT routines (memset/memcpy, x87 math) are normal; look for gaps containing API-walking code.
- Rarely-called exports (operator helpers, debug and utility functions) are favourite stomp targets: overwriting them doesn't break the host's normal use.

## 3. Recognise injected loader idioms
- PE export walk: `[base+0x3C]` → NT, `+0x88` export dir (x64), then +0x18/+0x1C/+0x20/+0x24 (NumberOfNames, AddressOfFunctions, AddressOfNames, AddressOfNameOrdinals).
- Hash loop over a name followed by `cmp edx, rXd` against constants from data. Recover the algorithm and seed, then resolve the hashes statically against the local system DLL export names (read files only).
- `GetModuleFileNameW` + scan back to `\` + `SetCurrentDirectoryW` means the loader is anchored to the host EXE folder (sideloading), and a payload file probably sits next to it.
- `LoadLibrary(sacrificial) → VirtualProtect(BaseOfCode, RWX) → memcpy → call` is **module stomping**.
- Huge, side-effect-free nested loops early in the chain are time-based sandbox evasion.

## 4. Data-side tampering
- Packed, unaligned globals (fields at odd addresses), and strings written over function-pointer tables, show attacker-added config in .data. Decode them by following every RIP-relative read in the injected code.

## 5. Ghidra MCP workflow notes
- Read-only sessions can't create functions. Open a **writable session on a copy** to `disassemble_seed` (with clear_existing) from the true entry and rebuild the function.
- Ghidra auto-creates bogus functions at stomped export addresses. Trust a fresh linear/flow disassembly from the real prologue instead.
- To find the trigger, scan rel32 calls/jumps, RIP-relative disp32 (any instruction ending in disp), absolute qword pointers, 4-byte RVAs (exports, CFG table, unwind handlers) and TLS callbacks. If nothing references the entry, the trigger is probably external (the host).

## 6. Tool notes
- capa can fail with "memory allocation … failed" when disk or RAM is low; free space and re-run, or mark it UNAVAILABLE.
- FLOSS works on files under 16 MB; decoded/tight strings are often noise for loaders that keep config in plain data.

## Verdict: MALWARE, a trojanized Intel-signed DLL that loads shellcode via sideloading. Confidence: high.

This is a genuine Intel `ForOps.dll` (Intel Fortran Utility Package 2025.1.1.0) that someone edited after Intel signed it, and it now carries a hidden shellcode loader. I analysed it with static tools only; nothing was executed or loaded.

**Strongest evidence**
- **Tampered after signing.** The Intel signature (Sectigo-issued, timestamped 2025-03-28) reports HashMismatch: the signed digest `9FED12F9…EE75` doesn't match the file's actual hash `10F06374…FC48`. The PE checksum doesn't match either, and nothing is appended, so the edits are inside the signed sections.
- **Code overwritten inside the DLL.** About 1.9 KB of code (RVA 0x55F0–0x5D6F) was replaced. That region originally held 20 small exported Fortran helpers (`and_*`, `or_*`, `xor_*`, `eqv_*`) plus `uminus_cplx32`. The unwind table still lists those original functions, but each listed start now lands mid-instruction in new code.
- **Sandbox-evasion delay** at 0x1800055F0: a pointless loop of about 1.8 billion iterations that only burns CPU time.
- **The loader itself**, at 0x180005760:
  1. resolves APIs by hash (seed 0x0761F9B7, `h = h*2 + c`); all eight hashes resolved: LocalAlloc, SetCurrentDirectoryW, CreateFileA, GetFileSize, ReadFile, LoadLibraryA, VirtualProtect, TerminateProcess;
  2. switches to the folder of the program that loaded it and reads **`compiler128.sys`** from there, terminating the process if the file is empty;
  3. decodes the data at offset 0x4D42 with an additive dword key;
  4. loads a decoy DLL (named inside the encrypted file), makes that DLL's code area writable and executable, overwrites it with the decoded shellcode, and runs it with the argument `console-io.yaml`. This technique is called module stomping.
- **Configuration planted in `.data`:** a packed block of settings, with `console-io.yaml` written over the DLL's own operator-function table, so it can no longer work as the real Intel library.
- **Everything else is genuine Intel code:** `DllMain`, the startup routines, the imports, and the `.trace` debug data.

**Key IOCs**
- DLL SHA256 `8E8F0DA12204B277539590DDD30A78CE3943355FD1F8BD9DB71E4272BE71C4BC` (MD5 `AA91901CCE91F160E64B6187EF96EBE5`)
- Payload file **`compiler128.sys`**, in the same folder as the host program; argument string `console-io.yaml`
- Abused Intel signing certificate: thumbprint `5E4AE5E468F6D28D90C48DB09DCB672C2AD5EE4D`
- Detection byte pattern (hash loop): `0F B6 C0 48 8D 49 01 8D 14 50 0F B6 01 84 C0 75 EF`, together with the seed bytes `B7 F9 61 07`

**Detection justification:** The file passes as "Intel-signed" at a glance, but its signature is broken, and the bytes that changed are a self-contained loader. That loader evades sandboxes, resolves APIs by hash, decodes a payload file kept next to the host program, and runs it from inside another DLL's memory. No legitimate Intel component does any of that, so detecting it as malware is justified. Flagging Intel-signed `ForOps*.dll` files whose signature check fails is a high-fidelity rule for this pattern.

**Uncertainties**
- **The trigger isn't confirmed.** Nothing inside the DLL calls the loader at 0x180005760. Most likely the program that sideloads it calls into the overwritten area, but that needs the host program or dynamic analysis to prove.
- **Payload not available.** `compiler128.sys` wasn't provided, so the final payload, and the decoy DLL named inside it, are unknown.
- **No clean copy to compare against.** I found the edited region by structure, not by a byte-for-byte diff, so smaller edits elsewhere can't be fully ruled out.
- **Two pipeline tools didn't run.** capa failed for lack of memory (the disk was nearly full when it ran), and PEstats is missing the `pefile` package. FLOSS and DIE ran; DIE labels the compiler MSVC, but Ghidra and the file structure point to clang.

**Disk space:** to free space I deleted `C:\dyn_53AE\out\capture.csv` (1.9 GB). It was my own export from the earlier Datto run, and the original `.pml` capture files are still there if you need it again.

- Reusable techniques: `C:\Users\pandalabs\Desktop\Tools\Analysis\AA91901CCE91F160E64B6187EF96EBE5_analysis\skill.md`

# Skill: Triaging proxy (side-load) DLLs with embedded encrypted payloads

Generic and reusable; no sample-specific IOCs.

## 1. Spot a proxy DLL fast
- Parse the export directory: exports whose RVA falls inside the export directory are **forwarders**. Forwarders pointing at `<originalname><random>.dll` (or `<name>_orig.dll`) mean the real DLL was renamed and this file sits in its place.
- Also check the imports: a proxy often imports from the renamed original too (`jmp [IAT]` thunks).
- The **locally implemented** exports are the interesting ones. The one with a register/flag-preserving stub (`pushad; pushfd; call X; mov [esp+20h],eax; popfd; popad; jmp eax`) is the trigger: it resolves the real export, runs the payload, then tail-jumps to the real function so the host keeps working.
- Unsigned files carrying a vendor's version info are a red flag when the vendor normally signs.

## 2. Entropy and size heuristics
- A multi-MB `.rdata` with entropy ≈ 7.0 in a utility DLL means an embedded encrypted blob. Look for a chunk table (offset/size pairs) with a bound check that equals roughly the blob size.

## 3. Common loader stages to recognise
- One-time execution gate: a spin-lock flag plus a **loader-lock check** (TEB→PEB+0xA0 `LoaderLock` on x86, `RecursionCount` and `OwningThread` vs `TEB.ClientId.UniqueThread`). This shows the author avoided running heavy code inside DllMain.
- Self-path discovery: `GetModuleFileNameW(hSelf)` (hModule saved in DllMain), cut at the last `\`, then load companion files from the same folder.
- Custom `GetProcAddress`: `e_lfanew` (+0x3C) → export dir (+0x78 on x86, +0x88 on x64).
- Multi-stage decrypt: per-byte rotate/add → PRNG keystream XOR (64-bit multiply/xorshift constants) → more rounds. The `MZ`/`PE\0\0` checks after decryption confirm a PE payload. Per-section hash tables mean integrity checks before mapping.
- A manual mapper calling many helpers (sections, relocations, imports, TLS, protections, entry) means reflective loading (T1620).

## 4. Rust-specific tells
- Imports `NtWriteFile`, `RtlNtStatusToDosError`, `WriteConsoleW`, `GetConsoleMode`, plus the string `Local\RustBacktraceMutex`, mean Rust std. `CreateMutexA` for that mutex is benign runtime behaviour.
- Scrambled panic-location strings (random lowercase words next to line numbers) suggest build-time string obfuscation.

## 5. Working with huge decompiler output
- The Ghidra MCP may persist very large decompilations to a file. Process them with a script: list call targets, constants, data refs and key line ranges instead of reading everything.

## 6. When static decryption stalls
- If a key is produced by an obfuscated earlier stage, document the algorithm and constants. Then recommend emulating that stage (Unicorn/Qiling in isolation) or a controlled dynamic dump right after the MZ/PE validation.

# Skill: Triaging proxy (side-load) DLLs with embedded encrypted payloads

Generic and reusable; no sample-specific IOCs.

## 1. Spot a proxy DLL fast
- Parse the export directory: exports whose RVA falls inside the export directory are **forwarders**. Forwarders pointing at `<originalname><random>.dll` (or `<name>_orig.dll`) mean the real DLL was renamed and this file sits in its place.
- Also check the imports: a proxy often imports from the renamed original too (`jmp [IAT]` thunks).
- The **locally implemented** exports are the interesting ones. The one with a register/flag-preserving stub (`pushad; pushfd; call X; mov [esp+20h],eax; popfd; popad; jmp eax`) is the trigger: it resolves the real export, runs the payload, then tail-jumps to the real function so the host keeps working.
- Unsigned files carrying a vendor's version info are a red flag when the vendor normally signs.

## 2. Entropy and size heuristics
- A multi-MB `.rdata` with entropy ≈ 7.0 in a utility DLL means an embedded encrypted blob. Look for a chunk table (offset/size pairs) with a bound check that equals roughly the blob size.

## 3. Common loader stages to recognise
- One-time execution gate: a spin-lock flag plus a **loader-lock check** (TEB→PEB+0xA0 `LoaderLock` on x86, `RecursionCount` and `OwningThread` vs `TEB.ClientId.UniqueThread`). This shows the author avoided running heavy code inside DllMain.
- Self-path discovery: `GetModuleFileNameW(hSelf)` (hModule saved in DllMain), cut at the last `\`, then load companion files from the same folder.
- Custom `GetProcAddress`: `e_lfanew` (+0x3C) → export dir (+0x78 on x86, +0x88 on x64).
- Multi-stage decrypt: per-byte rotate/add → PRNG keystream XOR (64-bit multiply/xorshift constants) → more rounds. The `MZ`/`PE\0\0` checks after decryption confirm a PE payload. Per-section hash tables mean integrity checks before mapping.
- A manual mapper calling many helpers (sections, relocations, imports, TLS, protections, entry) means reflective loading (T1620).

## 4. Rust-specific tells
- Imports `NtWriteFile`, `RtlNtStatusToDosError`, `WriteConsoleW`, `GetConsoleMode`, plus the string `Local\RustBacktraceMutex`, mean Rust std. `CreateMutexA` for that mutex is benign runtime behaviour.
- Scrambled panic-location strings (random lowercase words next to line numbers) suggest build-time string obfuscation.

## 5. Working with huge decompiler output
- The Ghidra MCP may persist very large decompilations to a file. Process them with a script: list call targets, constants, data refs and key line ranges instead of reading everything.

## 6. When static decryption stalls
- If a key is produced by an obfuscated earlier stage, document the algorithm and constants. Then recommend emulating that stage (Unicorn/Qiling in isolation) or a controlled dynamic dump right after the MZ/PE validation.

## Verdict: MALWARE, a fake Alibaba `arphaDump.dll` that hijacks a legitimate app to load a hidden second-stage program into memory. Confidence: high.

The file poses as Alibaba's `arphaDump.dll` (crash-dump SDK 3.1.6). It is built in Rust, it is unsigned, and it is meant to be dropped in place of the real DLL next to an Alibaba application. I analysed it statically only; nothing was executed.

**Strongest evidence**
- **It sits in front of the real DLL.** The real `arphaDump.dll` has been renamed to `arphaDumpvasugetduuziil.dll`, and this fake passes 5 of its 8 functions straight through to it. `GetArphaApp` does the same. Only `GetArphaUtils` and an exported `DllMain` contain the fake's own code.
- **`GetArphaUtils` is the trigger.** It saves all registers and flags, then calls a hidden routine (0x1004BF35) that:
  - finds its own folder and loads the renamed real DLL from there;
  - looks up the real `GetArphaUtils` with its own export-lookup code and jumps to it, so the host app keeps working normally;
  - runs the payload once, and only after `DllMain` has finished (it checks the Windows loader lock first);
  - kills the process with exit code `0xD5BF` if an early check fails.
- **The payload is an encrypted program hidden in the DLL** (routine at 0x10045F3E). The DLL's 2.2 MB read-only data section is almost random (entropy 7.01). The routine:
  1. reassembles 14 encrypted pieces from that data;
  2. decrypts them in three stages: a per-byte rotation, an XOR with a generated key stream, then four more mixing rounds;
  3. checks that the result is a valid Windows program (`MZ` and `PE` headers) and verifies a checksum for each of its sections;
  4. loads and runs it directly in memory, never writing it to disk.
- **Deliberate anti-analysis:** a computed-jump dispatcher, junk code in `DllMain`, encrypted strings, scrambled Rust error-location strings, and API lookups that bypass the normal import table.

**Key IOCs**
- DLL SHA256 `F0F715A52DE3958935A04FB75D7D02FFA73BF4E1D6480B0AC6FF1DF24A3590AC` (MD5 `BC1A344653D707928E281CBA199355CF`)
- An unsigned `arphaDump.dll` with **`arphaDumpvasugetduuziil.dll` beside it**; the pair is the strongest field indicator
- Trigger export `GetArphaUtils`; exit code `0xD5BF`
- Decoded strings `anticheat-vm-build-id-v1`, `dwqyeoikydpz`, `X1407551829`
- Byte pattern of the `GetArphaUtils` stub: `60 9C E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? 89 44 24 20 9D 61 FF E0`

**Detection justification:** Every real function call is forwarded to a randomly renamed copy of the vendor DLL. The only code of its own decrypts an embedded program, checks its integrity, and runs it in memory. A genuine crash-dump SDK does none of this, so detecting it as malware is justified. The unsigned `arphaDump.dll` plus `arphaDump<random>.dll` pair is a reliable detection rule.

**Uncertainties**
- **The hidden program wasn't decrypted.** Its key comes from another obfuscated stage I didn't reimplement, so its family and capabilities are unknown. To identify it, dump it at the point where the loader validates the decrypted program, or emulate the key-derivation routine (0x10036058) in an isolated environment.
- **The host application wasn't provided.** It's probably a legitimate Alibaba app (for example DingTalk) that loads `arphaDump.dll`.
- **`anticheat-vm-build-id-v1`'s role is a guess.** It looks like a label used in key derivation or an integrity check; it doesn't by itself mean a real anti-cheat product is involved.
- **Two pipeline tools have no results.** capa was still running when I wrote the report; PEstats is missing the `pefile` package. DIE and FLOSS ran.

# Static Analysis Report — BC1A344653D707928E281CBA199355CF

**Verdict:** MALWARE — malicious **proxy DLL for side-loading** posing as Alibaba `arphaDump.dll`; a Rust-built **in-memory PE loader** carrying an encrypted second stage
**Confidence:** High
**Analysis type:** Static only (Ghidra headless MCP, DIE, FLOSS, header parsing). Nothing was executed.

---

## 1. Metadata

| Field | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| MD5 / SHA256 | BC1A344653D707928E281CBA199355CF / F0F715A52DE3958935A04FB75D7D02FFA73BF4E1D6480B0AC6FF1DF24A3590AC | [CONFIRMED] |
| Size | 2,819,584 bytes | |
| Type | PE32 x86 DLL, image base 0x10000000, 5 sections, MSVC 19.39 / VS2022 17.9 linker; Rust std runtime (`Local\RustBacktraceMutex`, NtWriteFile/RtlNtStatusToDosError imports) | DIE, FLOSS, imports |
| PE timestamp | 2024-06-16 09:49:42 UTC | header |
| Version info | Alibaba Group, product `arphasdk`, `arphaDump.dll` 3.1.6, "Copyright (C) 2017 Alibaba Group" | VersionInfo |
| Signature | **NotSigned** (genuine arpha components are vendor-signed [INFERRED]) | Authenticode |
| Overlay | none | |

**Section entropy:** `.text` 0x7B800 bytes, H = 7.01 · **`.rdata` 0x230800 bytes (2.2 MB), H = 7.01** · `.data` 2.49 · `.rsrc` 3.87 · `.reloc` 6.68. The high-entropy `.rdata` holds the encrypted payload (the chunks are read below offset 0x153926).

## 2. Ranked findings

1. **[CONFIRMED] Proxy / side-load DLL.** The export DLL name is `arphaDump.dll`. 5 of 8 exports are **forwarders to `arphaDumpvasugetduuziil.dll`**, the genuine DLL renamed: `GetArphaCrashDump`, `GetArphaCrashReport`, `GetArphaJamDump`, `GetArphaService` and `SetWindowLocalDump`. `GetArphaApp` (0x1007AAA0) is `jmp [IAT]` into the same renamed DLL. Only **`GetArphaUtils` (0x10001090)** and an exported **`DllMain`** (0x1004BEB7) are local code.
2. **[CONFIRMED] Trigger = `GetArphaUtils`.** `pushad; pushfd; call 0x1004BF35; mov [esp+0x20],eax; popfd; popad; jmp eax`. The dispatcher at 0x1004BF35:
   - decodes obfuscated strings (rotate + subtract-key and modular-inverse multiply loops);
   - runs `GetModuleFileNameW(hSelf)` (hModule saved by `DllMain`), cuts at the last `\` and loads the renamed original from the **same folder**;
   - resolves the real `GetArphaUtils` with a custom export walker (`FUN_1005CC55`), caches it (`DAT_102AEF7C`) and jumps to it so the host keeps working;
   - **runs the payload routine `FUN_10045F3E` once** (spin-lock `DAT_102AEF78`), and only if `FUN_1000E5D9` reports the thread is **not holding the loader lock** (TEB→PEB+0xA0 `LoaderLock.OwningThread` vs `ClientId.UniqueThread`);
   - calls `ExitProcess(0xD5BF)` if an early check (`FUN_1005C12F`) fails.
3. **[CONFIRMED] Encrypted in-memory PE loader (`FUN_10045F3E`, 0x10045F3E–0x1004BEB6):**
   1. reassembles **14 chunks** (offset/size table, each bounded by 0x153926, total length checked) from the embedded blob;
   2. per-byte rotate decode `((b+0x70)>>3) | (b<<5)`;
   3. XOR with a 64-bit multiply/xorshift keystream (constants 0x62175881, 0x22E816E4, 0x62485F5F, 0x7770EB58, 0x548DACF3, 0x44471CE1), seeded by the return value of `FUN_10035F8C` (aborts if 0);
   4. four further rotate/multiply rounds (constants 0xB8F74423, 0xD7360B06, 0x1D41FBD5, 0x1CE4E5B9, 0x133111EB);
   5. validates **`MZ` (0x5A4D) and `PE\0\0` (0x4550)**;
   6. verifies per-section hashes against a table at 0x100817C0 (FNV-like, seed 0x89EEB54F / 0xE5978918, multiplier 0x4835C209), an integrity/anti-tamper check;
   7. manual-maps and runs it via `FUN_100562CB`, about 25 helpers typical of a reflective/manual PE loader;
   8. wipes the buffers.
4. **[CONFIRMED] Anti-analysis and obfuscation:** a computed-jump dispatcher with register/flag preservation; junk arithmetic in `DllMain`; encrypted stack strings; scrambled Rust panic-location strings (`ewsqdzalxg`, `vkodjhbjzzhksequbmgg`); dynamic API resolution through export walking; Rust-std imports only (no suspicious APIs in the IAT apart from `VirtualProtect`).
5. **[INFERRED] FLOSS-decoded string `anticheat-vm-build-id-v1`.** Likely a KDF/integrity context label used by the decryption stage. Other decoded strings: `dwqyeoikydpz`, `X1407551829`.
6. capa: **PENDING/UNAVAILABLE** when this report was written. PEstats: **UNAVAILABLE** (`pefile` missing).
7. No text addressed to an AI was found.

## 3. Function table

| Address | Name | Role |
|---|---|---|
| 0x1006C240 | entry | MSVC CRT DllMainCRTStartup |
| 0x1004BEB7 | DllMain (exported) | Saves hModule → `DAT_102AEFD4`; junk loop |
| 0x1007AAA0 | GetArphaApp | `jmp [IAT]` → renamed original |
| **0x10001090** | **GetArphaUtils** | Trigger stub (pushad/pushfd/call/jmp eax) |
| **0x1004BF35** | resolve_and_dispatch | String decode, load renamed DLL, resolve real export, gate + run payload once |
| 0x1000E5D9 | not_under_loader_lock | TEB/PEB LoaderLock owner check |
| **0x10045F3E** | **payload_decrypt_and_run** | 14-chunk reassembly, 3-stage decrypt, MZ/PE + hash check, map |
| 0x100562CB | manual_map_pe | Section map / relocations / imports / entry |
| 0x1005CC55 | custom_GetProcAddress | Export-table walker |
| 0x10035F8C → 0x10036058 | stage key derivation | Produces the 64-bit XOR seed |

## 4. IOCs

| Type | Value |
|---|---|
| SHA256 | F0F715A52DE3958935A04FB75D7D02FFA73BF4E1D6480B0AC6FF1DF24A3590AC |
| Masquerade name | `arphaDump.dll` (Alibaba Group, arphasdk 3.1.6), unsigned |
| **Renamed original (must sit beside it)** | `arphaDumpvasugetduuziil.dll` |
| Trigger export | `GetArphaUtils` |
| Exit code on failed check | 0xD5BF |
| Decoded strings | `anticheat-vm-build-id-v1`, `dwqyeoikydpz`, `X1407551829` |
| Payload location | `.rdata` file 0x07BC00+ (2.2 MB, H 7.01); chunk bound 0x153926 |
| Section-hash table | VA 0x100817C0 |

## 5. ATT&CK

T1574.002 DLL Side-Loading [CONFIRMED by proxy design] · T1036.005 Masquerading: match legitimate name (Alibaba arphaDump) [CONFIRMED] · T1027 / T1140 encrypted embedded payload + runtime decode [CONFIRMED] · T1027.007 dynamic API resolution [CONFIRMED] · T1620 Reflective Code Loading (manual-mapped PE) [CONFIRMED] · T1622 / T1497 anti-analysis checks [INFERRED]

## 6. Alternative hypotheses

| Hypothesis | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Legitimate Alibaba arphaDump | **Rejected**: unsigned, forwards to a renamed original, and contains an encrypted PE loader |
| Game anti-cheat / software protector (`anticheat-vm-build-id-v1`) | Considered. A commercial protector wraps its own code; it does not proxy a third-party crash-dump DLL to a randomly renamed original. That pattern is side-loading malware |
| Red-team loader | Possible origin; still functionally malicious |

## 7. Limitations

- The second-stage PE was **not decrypted statically**: the 64-bit XOR seed comes from an obfuscated stage (`FUN_10036058`), and the chunk table is built from obfuscated arithmetic. Its family and capabilities are unknown.
- The host EXE is not provided. It is likely a legitimate Alibaba application (for example DingTalk) that imports `arphaDump.dll`. [HYPOTHESIS]
- capa pending; PEstats unavailable.

## 8. Next steps

1. Hunt `arphaDumpvasugetduuziil.dll` next to any `arphaDump.dll` (the renamed-original pair is a strong indicator). Collect the host EXE and folder.
2. Dynamic analysis (not performed): run the host in an isolated VM, break after `FUN_10045F3E`'s MZ/PE check or on the mapped image's entry, and dump the decrypted PE for family identification.
3. Optional static next step: emulate `FUN_10036058` and the chunk-table arithmetic (for example with Unicorn/Qiling in an isolated environment) to decrypt the payload offline.

## 9. Detection

- Unsigned `arphaDump.dll` exporting forwarders to `arphaDump<random>.dll`.
- The `GetArphaUtils` stub bytes `60 9C E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? 89 44 24 20 9D 61 FF E0`.
- The rotate-decode loop and keystream constants 0x62175881 / 0x62485F5F / 0x548DACF3 in a ~2.8 MB x86 DLL.

capa finished and supports the **MALWARE** verdict without changing it. Its matches line up with what I found in Ghidra:

- **The proxying and lookup tricks:** it flags the forwarded exports, the API lookups done by reading DLL export tables, the runtime linking, and the direct reads of the Windows process block (PEB) that the loader-lock check uses.
- **The in-memory loader:** it flags PE header parsing, walking the sections, changing memory protection, and read/write memory allocation.
- **Anti-analysis:** it flags a check for software breakpoints and references to analysis-tool names.
- **More encryption than I had seen:** it also detects AES (using the CPU's AES instructions), SHA256, RC4 and murmur3 hashing. The custom decryption stages I decompiled don't use these. They most likely sit in the key-derivation stage I didn't decrypt (0x10036058), which suggests the hidden second-stage program is protected by AES with a SHA256-derived key.

I added these results to section 2 of `C:\Users\pandalabs\Desktop\Tools\Analysis\BC1A344653D707928E281CBA199355CF_analysis\report.md`. PEstats still has no output because the `pefile` package is missing from the venv; installing it with `pip install pefile` would fix that for future samples.

**Verdict: MALWARE (Trojan: DLL side-loading loader), high confidence**

`BC1A344653D707928E281CBA199355CF` is an unsigned Rust-built DLL that poses as Alibaba's `arphaDump.dll` and replaces it next to a legitimate application. It passes almost every function through to the real DLL, renamed to `arphaDumpvasugetduuziil.dll`, so the host app keeps working. When the app calls `GetArphaUtils`, an obfuscated routine runs once. It reassembles an encrypted program from a 2.2 MB near-random data blob, decrypts it in several stages, checks that it is a valid program, and loads and runs it directly in memory. capa independently found the same behaviour: API lookups through DLL export tables, PE parsing and memory-protection changes, AES, SHA256 and RC4, a software-breakpoint check, and references to analysis tools. A real crash-dump SDK does none of this. The finished second-stage program wasn't decrypted, so its family is still unknown.

If you meant the earlier samples too:
- `53AEBACA7DF9F95E57F96A9F9E09E09B` is LEGITIMATE but dual-use (Datto RMM agent, PUA/RemoteAdmin by policy).
- `AA91901CCE91F160E64B6187EF96EBE5` is MALWARE (a trojanized Intel-signed `ForOps.dll` shellcode loader).

# Skill: Static triage of .NET binaries without a working decompiler CLI

Generic; no sample-specific IOCs.

## 1. Headless decompilation pitfalls
- `dnSpy.Console.exe` crashes with `IOException: The handle is invalid` at `Console.set_OutputEncoding` when the shell gives it no real console, even under `cmd /c` or `Start-Process`. Don't loop on it.
- Fallback: build a tiny .NET console app against **dnlib.dll** (ships with dnSpy in `bin\`). `ModuleDefMD.Load(File.ReadAllBytes(path))` only parses bytes; it never loads the assembly into the runtime. Dump:
  - assembly refs, attributes, entry point;
  - types/methods with instruction counts and P/Invoke `ImplMap` (DLL!function);
  - IL with resolved operands (`IMethod.FullName`, ldstr strings);
  - the #US user-string heap;
  - embedded resources to files.
- The .NET SDK builds such a project offline (no NuGet needed when referencing a local DLL by HintPath).

## 2. Fast identification
- The entry-point namespace and command classes usually reveal public tooling (for example `Certify.*`, `Rubeus.*`, `Seatbelt.*`) even when the assembly/product name has been changed.
- P/Invoke lists summarise capabilities quickly: token APIs = impersonation; SSPI = NTLM/Kerberos auth; DCOM `CoCreateInstanceEx` = remote COM; crypt32 PFX APIs = certificate export.

## 3. Embedded dependency loaders
- `<Module>.cctor` → an AssemblyResolve handler + `GetManifestResourceStream` + decompress + `Assembly.Load(byte[])` is a dependency bundler (Costura/Fody-like).
- Resource header `5D 00 00 80 00` = LZMA "alone" format; Python `lzma.decompress(data, format=lzma.FORMAT_ALONE)` unpacks it statically.
- Always unpack and identify every embedded assembly (VersionInfo, hash). Bundlers are also used to hide extra payloads, so check that each is the expected third-party library.

## 4. Hacktool vs trojanized hacktool
- Scan the IL for behaviour outside the tool's purpose: `Process.Start`, sockets/WebClient, `VirtualAlloc`/`CreateThread` P/Invokes, persistence (Run keys, scheduled tasks), extra `Assembly.Load` of non-library blobs. If there is none, classify it as HackTool (context decides malice). Otherwise treat it as malware wrapping a hacktool.

I've compared that IDA AI report and triage with my analysis. **My verdict stays MALWARE (side-loading loader).** The IDA verdict of LEGITIMATE (96%, score 0/100) comes from analysing the wrong code: it spent its budget on the Rust and MSVC runtime and never reached the payload routine.

**Why the IDA result is wrong**

| Issue in the IDA output | What the binary actually shows |
|---|---|
| Its code-origin step labels **98.5% of functions "unclassified (treated as author)"**, with only 1 confirmed author function | It didn't recognise Rust's standard library. Most of its findings are Rust or CRT internals: lookups of `NtCreateKeyedEvent`/`NtWaitForKeyedEvent`/`NtReleaseKeyedEvent` and `WaitOnAddress` (Rust's thread synchronisation), `SymSetSearchPathW`/`StackWalkEx` (Rust's panic backtrace via dbghelp), `CorExitProcess` (CRT exit), and the `IsDebuggerPresent`/`IsProcessorFeaturePresent` failure path (MSVC CRT). |
| It lists IOC `Local\RustBacktraceMutex00000000` | That's a normal Rust runtime mutex, not an indicator of compromise. |
| Its own triage flags **"side-loading hint: 5 forwarded exports (proxy DLL pattern)"** but marks it uncorroborated | My analysis corroborates it: the 5 forwarded exports go to the renamed original `arphaDumpvasugetduuziil.dll`, and `GetArphaApp` is a jump into that same DLL. |
| It reports `sub_1004BF35` uses `lock cmpxchg` on `dword_102AEF78` and stores to `dword_102AEF7C`, but calls the purpose "not established" | That's the run-once gate. Right after it, the routine checks the loader lock and calls **`FUN_10045F3E`, the payload routine.** None of the 58 functions IDA analysed is `0x10045F3E`. |
| It says the routine "ultimately calls ExitProcess(0xD5BF)" | That's only the branch taken when a check fails. The normal path loads the real DLL from the same folder, jumps to its `GetArphaUtils`, and runs the payload once. |
| "Packing: none" | It reads only packer signatures. `.rdata` is **2.2 MB with entropy 7.01**, the encrypted payload, which `FUN_10045F3E` rebuilds from 14 chunks and decrypts in three stages before checking for valid `MZ`/`PE` headers and loading it in memory. |
| No crypto or loader behaviour scored | capa on the same file finds **AES (CPU AES instructions), SHA256, RC4 and murmur3**, plus PE parsing, section enumeration, API lookups via DLL export tables, memory-protection changes, a software-breakpoint check, and references to analysis-tool names. None of that belongs in a crash-dump SDK. |
| "No family matched" | That's expected: the YARA rules can only see the plain loader, and the family is in the encrypted payload. |

**Bottom line:** An unsigned DLL using Alibaba's name and version info that forwards its real functions to a randomly renamed copy of the vendor DLL is a side-loading implant by design. The IDA triage noticed the proxy pattern but never analysed `FUN_10045F3E`, where the decryption and in-memory loading happen. Its LEGITIMATE verdict is a false negative caused by the gaps above. It would be worth reporting this to whoever maintains that engine:
- recognise Rust std and runtime code so it isn't counted as author code;
- score the forwarded-exports-to-a-renamed-DLL pattern;
- follow the call that runs after a run-once gate;
- treat large high-entropy data sections as possible encrypted payloads even when no packer is detected.

## 2. Ranked findings

1. **[CONFIRMED] Proxy / side-load DLL.** The export DLL name is `arphaDump.dll`. 5 of 8 exports are **forwarders to `arphaDumpvasugetduuziil.dll`**, the genuine DLL renamed: `GetArphaCrashDump`, `GetArphaCrashReport`, `GetArphaJamDump`, `GetArphaService` and `SetWindowLocalDump`. `GetArphaApp` (0x1007AAA0) is `jmp [IAT]` into the same renamed DLL. Only **`GetArphaUtils` (0x10001090)** and an exported **`DllMain`** (0x1004BEB7) are local code.
2. **[CONFIRMED] Trigger = `GetArphaUtils`.** `pushad; pushfd; call 0x1004BF35; mov [esp+0x20],eax; popfd; popad; jmp eax`. The dispatcher at 0x1004BF35:
   - decodes obfuscated strings (rotate + subtract-key and modular-inverse multiply loops);
   - runs `GetModuleFileNameW(hSelf)` (hModule saved by `DllMain`), cuts at the last `\` and loads the renamed original from the **same folder**;

   1. reassembles **14 chunks** (offset/size table, each bounded by 0x153926, total length checked) from the embedded blob;

I've compared that IDA AI report and triage with my analysis. **My verdict stays MALWARE (side-loading loader).** The IDA verdict of LEGITIMATE (96%, score 0/100) comes from analysing the wrong code: it spent its budget on the Rust and MSVC runtime and never reached the payload routine.

**Why the IDA result is wrong**

| Issue in the IDA output | What the binary actually shows |
|---|---|
| Its code-origin step labels **98.5% of functions "unclassified (treated as author)"**, with only 1 confirmed author function | It didn't recognise Rust's standard library. Most of its findings are Rust or CRT internals: lookups of `NtCreateKeyedEvent`/`NtWaitForKeyedEvent`/`NtReleaseKeyedEvent` and `WaitOnAddress` (Rust's thread synchronisation), `SymSetSearchPathW`/`StackWalkEx` (Rust's panic backtrace via dbghelp), `CorExitProcess` (CRT exit), and the `IsDebuggerPresent`/`IsProcessorFeaturePresent` failure path (MSVC CRT). |
| It lists IOC `Local\RustBacktraceMutex00000000` | That's a normal Rust runtime mutex, not an indicator of compromise. |
| Its own triage flags **"side-loading hint: 5 forwarded exports (proxy DLL pattern)"** but marks it uncorroborated | My analysis corroborates it: the 5 forwarded exports go to the renamed original `arphaDumpvasugetduuziil.dll`, and `GetArphaApp` is a jump into that same DLL. |
| It reports `sub_1004BF35` uses `lock cmpxchg` on `dword_102AEF78` and stores to `dword_102AEF7C`, but calls the purpose "not established" | That's the run-once gate. Right after it, the routine checks the loader lock and calls **`FUN_10045F3E`, the payload routine.** None of the 58 functions IDA analysed is `0x10045F3E`. |
| It says the routine "ultimately calls ExitProcess(0xD5BF)" | That's only the branch taken when a check fails. The normal path loads the real DLL from the same folder, jumps to its `GetArphaUtils`, and runs the payload once. |
| "Packing: none" | It reads only packer signatures. `.rdata` is **2.2 MB with entropy 7.01**, the encrypted payload, which `FUN_10045F3E` rebuilds from 14 chunks and decrypts in three stages before checking for valid `MZ`/`PE` headers and loading it in memory. |
| No crypto or loader behaviour scored | capa on the same file finds **AES (CPU AES instructions), SHA256, RC4 and murmur3**, plus PE parsing, section enumeration, API lookups via DLL export tables, memory-protection changes, a software-breakpoint check, and references to analysis-tool names. None of that belongs in a crash-dump SDK. |
| "No family matched" | That's expected: the YARA rules can only see the plain loader, and the family is in the encrypted payload. |

**Bottom line:** An unsigned DLL using Alibaba's name and version info that forwards its real functions to a randomly renamed copy of the vendor DLL is a side-loading implant by design. The IDA triage noticed the proxy pattern but never analysed `FUN_10045F3E`, where the decryption and in-memory loading happen. Its LEGITIMATE verdict is a false negative caused by the gaps above. It would be worth reporting this to whoever maintains that engine:
- recognise Rust std and runtime code so it isn't counted as author code;
- score the forwarded-exports-to-a-renamed-DLL pattern;
- follow the call that runs after a run-once gate;
- treat large high-entropy data sections as possible encrypted payloads even when no packer is detected.

"""Known-family marker hints (deterministic, offline, no YARA).

frameworks: config markers, protocol strings, class names, registry
locations. A family is reported only when at least ``minimum`` of its markers
are present (one is enough only for markers flagged ``unique``). Hits are

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FamilyHit:
    family: str
    kind: str
    markers: Tuple[str, ...]


def match_families(texts: Iterable[str]) -> Tuple[FamilyHit, ...]:
    corpus = [text.lower() for text in texts if isinstance(text, str) and text]
    joined = "\n".join(corpus)
    hits: List[FamilyHit] = []
    for rule in FAMILY_RULES:
        found = tuple(marker for marker in rule.markers if marker in joined)
        if len(found) >= rule.minimum or (found and any(marker in found for marker in rule.unique)):
            hits.append(FamilyHit(rule.family, rule.kind, found))
    hits.sort(key=lambda hit: -len(hit.markers))
    return tuple(hits)


def format_family_hits(hits: Sequence[FamilyHit]) -> str:
    if not hits:
        return ""
    return "Family hints (marker matches, not a verdict): " + "; ".join(
        "{0} [{1}]".format(hit.family, ", ".join(hit.markers[:4])) for hit in hits[:3]
    )

# --- known-family markers (hints) -------------------------------------
    family_hits = _family_hits(overview, pe)
    for hit in family_hits[:2]:
        weight = WEIGHTS["family_hint_pup"] if hit.kind == "pup" else WEIGHTS["family_hint"]
        evidence.append(VerdictEvidence(
            "family_hint", weight, "family hint {0}: markers {1}".format(hit.family, ", ".join(hit.markers[:4])), (), basis="inferred",
        ))
        sources.add("family")
        if hit.kind == "hacktool":
            behaviour_scored.add(bh.HACKTOOL)
        elif hit.kind == "pup":
            behaviour_scored.add(bh.PUP_BROWSER_HIJACK)

    # --- family rule pack (optional Malpedia / community YARA; empty when not installed) ------
    # A family rule is written from that family's own code or artefacts and was checked here
    # against System32/SysWOW64 and a clean set without a hit: it is decisive on its own,
    # except on a genuinely Microsoft-signed file (then it is only reported).
    rule_family_names: List[str] = []
    rule_family_hints: List[str] = []
    for hit in list(rule_hits)[:4]:
        functions = tuple("{0} (0x{1:X})".format(name, address) for address, name in getattr(hit, "functions", ())[:_MAX_ADDRESSES])
        user = bool(getattr(hit, "user", False))
        if user:
            # The analyst's own rule (user_rules.yar), written for this sample or its variants.
            origin = "your rule {0} ({1})".format(hit.rule, getattr(hit, "source", "") or "user_rules.yar")
        else:
            origin = "Malpedia {0} {1}".format("auto-generated code rule" if hit.auto else "curated rule", hit.rule)
        if microsoft_signed(pe):
            notes.append("family rule {0} matched a genuinely Microsoft-signed file - reported, not scored".format(hit.rule))
            continue
        evidence.append(VerdictEvidence(
            "known_family_code", WEIGHTS["known_family_code_auto"] if hit.auto and not user else WEIGHTS["known_family_code"],
            "known malware family {0}: {1} matched{2}".format(
                hit.display, origin, " - family-specific code in these functions" if functions else ""),
            functions, basis="observed",
        ))
        sources.add("rules")
        rule_family_names.append(hit.display)
        rule_family_hints.append("{0} ({1})".format(hit.display, origin))
        if hit.hacktool:
            behaviour_scored.add(bh.HACKTOOL)
            behaviour_strong.add(bh.HACKTOOL)
        else:
            behaviour_scored.add("known_family_code")
            behaviour_strong.add("known_family_code")

    # --- loader / crypter techniques (entry trampolines, manual PE walking, VB6 declares,
    #     shellcode stagers, raw-IP downloaders) --------------------------------------
    extra_evasion: List[str] = []
    for item, behaviour, strong, evasion in _loader_patterns(overview, pe, code, present):
        evidence.append(item)
        sources.add("code" if item.category in ("pe_walk", "stager") else "file")
        if behaviour:
            behaviour_scored.add(behaviour)
            scored_categories.add(behaviour)
        if strong:
            behaviour_strong.add(strong)
            behaviour_scored.add(strong)
        if evasion:
            extra_evasion.append(evasion)

    # Evasion that legitimate software practically never combines: resolved API hashing,
    # anti-analysis instructions and a malware family-marker match. Two of them corroborate
    # each other (independent deterministic sources).
    evasion_kinds = list(extra_evasion)
    if code is not None and any(item.api_hashes for item in code.functions):
        evasion_kinds.append("API hashing")
    if any(item.category == "anti_analysis" and item.description.startswith("anti-analysis instructions") for item in evidence):
        evasion_kinds.append("anti-analysis instructions")
    if any(hit.kind in ("malware", "hacktool") for hit in family_hits):
        evasion_kinds.append("family markers")
    if len(evasion_kinds) >= 2 and microsoft_signed(pe):
        # Heuristic code signals (PE walking, anti-analysis instructions, coverage) appear in OS
        # code too; on a genuine Microsoft signature they are not evidence of evasion.
        notes.append("evasion heuristics ({0}) not scored: genuine Microsoft signature".format(" + ".join(evasion_kinds)))
    elif len(evasion_kinds) >= 2:
        behaviour_scored.add("evasive_code")
        behaviour_strong.add("evasive_code")
        notes.append("corroborated evasion: " + " + ".join(evasion_kinds))

    # --- mitigating signals --------------------------------------------
    index = getattr(overview, "origin_index", None)
    if index is not None and index.total:
        library_count = index.total - index.author_count
        library_ratio = library_count / float(index.total)
    else:
        library_count = sum(1 for item in overview.functions if item.is_library)
        library_ratio = (library_count / float(function_count)) if function_count else 0.0
    flirt_count = sum(1 for item in overview.functions if item.is_library)
    flirt_ratio = (flirt_count / float(len(overview.functions))) if overview.functions else 0.0
    if language in STATIC_RUNTIME_LANGUAGES:
        notes.append(
            "library ratio {0:.0%} is normal for a statically linked {1} binary and is not used as a benign signal".format(library_ratio, language)
        )
    elif overview.functions and flirt_ratio > HIGH_LIBRARY_RATIO and not (behaviour_scored & bh.MALWARE_CATEGORIES):
        mitigating.append(
            VerdictEvidence("library_code", WEIGHTS["high_library_ratio"], "{0:.0%} of functions are library/FLIRT code ({1}/{2})".format(flirt_ratio, flirt_count, len(overview.functions)))
        )
    signer_text = "{0} {1}".format(getattr(pe, "signer", "") or "", getattr(pe, "signer_issuer", "") or "").lower() if pe is not None else ""
    fictional = pe is not None and getattr(pe, "signed", False) and any(name in signer_text for name in _FICTIONAL_PUBLISHERS)
    self_signed = (pe is not None and getattr(pe, "signed", False) and bool(getattr(pe, "signer", ""))
                   and (getattr(pe, "signer", "") or "").strip().lower() == (getattr(pe, "signer_issuer", "") or "").strip().lower())
    if fictional:
        evidence.append(VerdictEvidence("masquerade", 8, "signed with a fictional / test publisher name ({0}) - no real publisher stands behind it".format(
            getattr(pe, "signer", "") or "?")))
    if pe is not None and getattr(pe, "signed", False) and (fictional or self_signed):
        notes.append("signature not used as a benign signal: {0} certificate".format("fictional / test" if fictional else "self-signed"))
    elif pe is not None and getattr(pe, "signed", False):
        masquerade = any(getattr(item, "category", "") == "masquerade" for item in static)
        if not (behaviour_scored & bh.MALWARE_CATEGORIES) and "side_loading" not in behaviour_scored and not masquerade:
            mitigating.append(VerdictEvidence(
                "signature", WEIGHTS["signed_binary"],
                "Authenticode signature present{0} ({1})".format(
                    ": " + pe.signer if pe.signer else "",
                    "verified by Windows" if getattr(pe, "signature_verified", False) else "parsed, not cryptographically verified"),
            ))
        else:
            notes.append("signature present{0} but not used as a benign signal: malicious behaviour was corroborated (stolen or abused certificate?)".format(
                " (" + pe.signer + ")" if pe.signer else ""))
    author_count = index.author_count if index is not None else sum(1 for item in overview.functions if not item.is_library and not item.is_thunk)
    named_author = index.named_author_count if index is not None else 0
    if (
        index is not None
        and named_author >= 10
        and not behaviour_scored
        and not (scored_categories & SUSPICIOUS_CATEGORIES)
    ):
        mitigating.append(
            VerdictEvidence(
                "clean_author_code", WEIGHTS["clean_author_code"],
                "{0} named author functions inspected; none suggest malicious behaviour".format(named_author),
            )
        )
    gui_imports = sum(1 for item in overview.imports if item.dll.lower().split(".")[0] in GUI_DLLS)
    if (
        import_count > RICH_IAT_MIN_IMPORTS
        and gui_imports >= RICH_IAT_MIN_GUI_IMPORTS
        and not ({"injection", "network"} & scored_categories)
        and not (behaviour_scored & bh.MALWARE_CATEGORIES)
    ):
        mitigating.append(
            VerdictEvidence("plain_iat", WEIGHTS["rich_plain_iat"], "rich plain import table: {0} imports, {1} from GUI/CRT DLLs, no injection or networking".format(import_count, gui_imports))
        )
    version_hits = strings.get("version_info", [])
    if len(version_hits) >= 2:
        mitigating.append(
            VerdictEvidence("version_info", WEIGHTS["version_info"], "version information strings present: " + ", ".join(text for _, text in version_hits[:4]))
        )
    gui_coverage, gui_total = code_coverage(overview)
    if (
        all(present & group for group in BENIGN_GUI_APIS)
        and not (scored_categories & SUSPICIOUS_CATEGORIES)
        and not (behaviour_scored & bh.MALWARE_CATEGORIES)
        # A message loop is only a benign sign when the program's code is actually visible.
        and not getattr(pe, "entry_stub", "")
        and not (gui_total >= MIN_COVERAGE_BYTES and gui_coverage < MIN_CODE_COVERAGE)
        and not any(item.category == "entry_outside_code" or item.description.startswith("entry point in") for item in evidence)
    ):
        mitigating.append(
            VerdictEvidence("benign_gui", WEIGHTS["benign_gui"], "ordinary GUI message loop (CreateWindowEx + RegisterClass + DispatchMessage) with no suspicious API categories")
        )

    raw = sum(item.weight for item in evidence) + sum(item.weight for item in mitigating)
    score = _clamp(raw)
    malware_specific = behaviour_scored & _MALWARE_SPECIFIC
    strong_malware = behaviour_strong & _MALWARE_SPECIFIC
    if len(strong_malware) >= 2 or (strong_malware and len(malware_specific) >= 3) or bh.HACKTOOL in strong_malware:
        if score < STRONG_MULTI_FLOOR:
            notes.append("score raised to {0}: several malware behaviours corroborated by independent sources".format(STRONG_MULTI_FLOOR))
        score = max(score, STRONG_MULTI_FLOOR)
    elif strong_malware:
        if score < STRONG_SINGLE_FLOOR:
            notes.append("score raised to {0}: {1} corroborated by independent sources".format(
                STRONG_SINGLE_FLOOR, ", ".join(bh.CATEGORY_LABELS.get(item, item) for item in sorted(strong_malware))
            ))
        score = max(score, STRONG_SINGLE_FLOOR)
    # Windows-verified vendor signature and nothing but API capability: browsers' sandbox brokers,
    # updaters, debuggers and AV legitimately import injection / anti-debug APIs. Without any
    # corroborated malicious behaviour, family rule, malicious strings or evasive code the
    # capability is not intent. (A stolen certificate on real malware still fails this test: its
    # behaviour, strings or code signals are corroborated, which turns the cap off.)
    vendor_capped = False
    if (
        getattr(pe, "signature_verified", False)
        and not (fictional or self_signed)
        and not strong_malware
        and not (behaviour_scored & bh.MALWARE_CATEGORIES)
        and not rule_family_names
        and not any(hit.kind in ("malware", "hacktool") for hit in family_hits)
        and not any(item.category in ("masquerade", "static:masquerade") for item in evidence)
        and score > VENDOR_CAPABILITY_CAP
    ):
        notes.append("score capped at {0}: signature verified by Windows ({1}) and only API-capability evidence ({2}) - "
                     "no malicious behaviour, family rule, malicious strings or evasive code corroborated".format(
                         VENDOR_CAPABILITY_CAP, getattr(pe, "signer", "") or "signed",
                         ", ".join(sorted(scored_categories & SUSPICIOUS_CATEGORIES)) or "capabilities"))
        score = VENDOR_CAPABILITY_CAP
        vendor_capped = True
    pup_only = bool(behaviour_scored & bh.PUP_CATEGORIES) and not malware_specific and "injection" not in scored_categories

from ida_ai_malware_analyst_plugin.ida.compatibility import IdaModules, load_ida_modules


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TriageLimits:
    """Hard bounds that keep one triage pass compact even on very large IDBs."""

    #: Functions that get a full summary (instruction walk). Author code is
    #: summarized first, so a large runtime never crowds it out.
    max_functions: int = 6000
    #: Functions classified by name/flags only (cheap). Covers the whole IDB
    #: of any realistic sample, including 20k+ function Go/Rust binaries.
    max_inventory: int = 250000
    max_imports: int = 2000
    max_strings: int = 20000
    max_segments: int = 64
    min_string_length: int = 5
    max_entry_points: int = 256
    max_instructions_per_function: int = 2000
    max_callees_per_function: int = 32
    max_strings_per_function: int = 16
    max_xrefs_counted: int = 1000

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        for field_name, value in self.__dict__.items():
            if not isinstance(value, int) or isinstance(value, bool) or value <= 0:
                raise ValueError("{0} must be a positive integer".format(field_name))


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TriageModules:
    """Optional IDA modules used only by triage (kept out of ``IdaModules``)."""

    segment: Optional[ModuleType] = None
    entry: Optional[ModuleType] = None
    ida: Optional[ModuleType] = None

from ida_ai_malware_analyst_plugin.ida.code_reader import collect_code_signals

    author = [item for item in functions if item.origin in ANALYSABLE_ORIGINS and item.detailed and not item.is_thunk and item.size >= 16]
    # Named author code first, then the functions that call out the most (orchestrators), then the rest.
    author.sort(key=lambda item: (item.origin != "author", -(len(item.imports_called) + item.callee_count + item.string_count), item.address))

    def is_data(address: int) -> bool:
        segment = segment_index.find(address)
        return segment is not None and not segment.executable

    data_ranges = [(segment.start, segment.end) for segment in segments if not segment.executable and segment.size > 0]
    try:
        signals = collect_code_signals(modules, [(item.address, item.name) for item in author], data_ranges, is_data,
                                       max_instructions=limits.max_instructions_per_function)
    except Exception:  # code signals are an enhancement; triage must still complete
        return functions, strings, None
    by_address = {item.address: item for item in signals.functions}
    known = {item.address for item in strings}
    extra: List[StringInfo] = []
    updated: List[FunctionSummary] = []
    for item in functions:
        found = by_address.get(item.address)
        if found is None:
            updated.append(item)
            continue
        referenced = list(item.referenced_strings)
        for address, text, _method in found.decoded_strings:
            if text not in referenced and len(referenced) < limits.max_strings_per_function:
                referenced.append(text)
            if address not in known:
                known.add(address)
                extra.append(StringInfo(address=address, value=text))
        resolved = tuple(RESOLVED_API_PREFIX + entry[3].split("!", 1)[-1] for entry in found.api_hashes)
        updated.append(replace(
            item,
            referenced_strings=tuple(referenced),
            string_count=item.string_count + len(found.decoded_strings),
            imports_called=tuple(dict.fromkeys(item.imports_called + resolved)),
            signal_kinds=found.kinds,
        ))

"""Offline harness: run the IDA plugin's pure-Python static checks on sample files (no IDA, no execution).
usage: python -I plugin_static_test.py <plugin_root> <sample> [<sample> ...]
"""
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, sys.argv[1])
from ida_ai_malware_analyst_plugin.analysis import pe_static, family_markers, code_origin  # noqa: E402

for path in sys.argv[2:]:
    facts = pe_static.parse_pe_file(path)
    print("=" * 100)
    print(path)
    print("is_dll={0} dotnet={1} signed={2} export_dll={3!r}".format(facts.is_dll, facts.is_dotnet, facts.signed, facts.export_dll_name))
    for finding in pe_static.static_findings(facts):
        print("  [{0}] w={1}: {2}".format(finding.category, finding.weight, finding.description))
    # strings corpus for family markers / Rust detection (ASCII + UTF-16, like IDA's string list)
    import re
    data = open(path, "rb").read()
    strings = [m.group().decode("ascii") for m in re.finditer(rb"[\x20-\x7e]{5,}", data)]
    strings += [m.group().decode("utf-16le") for m in re.finditer(rb"(?:[\x20-\x7e]\x00){5,}", data)]
    hits = family_markers.match_families(strings)
    print("  family hits:", [(h.family, h.kind, h.markers[:4]) for h in hits] or "none")
    guess = code_origin.detect_language([], strings, [s.name for s in facts.sections], [])
    print("  language guess (strings/sections only):", guess.language, guess.confidence, guess.evidence)

            notes.append("score held in the PUP band: only adware / browser-hijack behaviour was corroborated")
